Central Nervous System
Anatomy
Scalp

Quick Overview

This lesson covers the scalp: the soft tissue covering the vault of the skull. It describes its extent, its five layers (with the clinically important connective tissue and "dangerous" loose areolar layers), the occipitofrontalis muscle, and its motor and sensory nerve supply and arterial supply. It closes with the opening general features of the face and the orbital part of orbicularis oculi.

Complete Lesson Content

Definition and extent

The scalp includes the soft tissues covering the vault of the skull.

  • Anteriorly: up to the eyebrows (superciliary arches).
  • Posteriorly: up to the superior nuchal lines.
  • Laterally (each side): up to the superior temporal line.

Layers of the scalp (S-C-A-L-P)

Five layers, from superficial to deep:

LayerKey features
1. SkinThick and hairy, with abundant sebaceous glands except over the forehead.
2. Connective tissue (superficial fascia)Dense fibrous tissue firmly binding skin to the underlying layer. Fibrous septa divide it into small pockets containing fat lobules. Blood vessels and nerves adhere to the septa.
3. Aponeurosis (epicranial aponeurosis / galea aponeurotica)Broad flat tendinous sheet connecting the frontal and occipital bellies of occipitofrontalis.
4. Loose areolar tissueTraversed by emissary veins connecting scalp veins (2nd layer) with intracranial dural venous sinuses.
5. PericraniumPeriosteum of the skull vault bones. Loosely attached to bone (easily stripped) but firmly attached at sutures to the sutural membrane.

Profuse bleeding: vessels in the connective tissue layer adhere to the fibrous septa, so when torn or cut they cannot retract.

Dangerous layer of the scalp (loose areolar tissue): blood and pus collect freely here. Pus can travel along emissary veins into the intracranial dural venous sinuses, causing thrombosis that may be fatal.

A hematoma in this layer tends to be generalized and blood extends to the upper eyelids, producing a black eye.

Occipitofrontalis muscle

A scalp muscle with 2 frontal and 2 occipital bellies.

  • Frontal bellies: arise from skin and subcutaneous tissue over the eyebrows and root of the nose; run backwards to insert into the epicranial aponeurosis in front of the coronal suture.
  • Occipital bellies: arise from the superior nuchal lines; extend forwards to insert into the epicranial aponeurosis. The two bellies are separated by a considerable gap filled by the aponeurosis.

Action

  • Frontal belly raises the eyebrows (as in surprise) and produces transverse wrinkles on the forehead.
  • Alternate contraction of frontal and occipital bellies moves the scalp forwards and backwards over the skull vault.

Nerve supply of the scalp

Motor supply, both in front of and behind the auricle, is from the facial nerve. Sensory supply in front of the auricle is from the trigeminal nerve; behind the auricle it is from cervical spinal nerves.

Motor

  • In front of the auricle: temporal branch of the facial nerve.
  • Behind the auricle: posterior auricular nerve.

Arterial supply of the scalp

Five arteries on each side: three in front of the auricle and two behind it.

In front of the auricle

  • Supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries: branches of the ophthalmic branch of the internal carotid; emerge from the orbit with their corresponding nerves.
  • Superficial temporal artery: one of the two terminal branches of the external carotid. It arises inside the parotid gland, emerges from its upper end, and divides into anterior and posterior divisions about 2 inches above the zygomatic arch. Its pulsation is felt in front of the tragus.

Branches of the superficial temporal artery:

  • Auricular branches to the anterior surface of the auricle.
  • Transverse facial artery: runs forwards below the zygomatic arch to supply the face.
  • Zygomatico-orbital artery: runs forwards above the zygomatic arch to supply the face.
  • Middle temporal artery.
  • Anterior (frontal) and posterior (parietal) divisions: terminal branches.

Behind the auricle (both from the external carotid)

  • Posterior auricular artery: reaches the back of the auricle; gives the important stylomastoid artery, which enters the stylomastoid foramen.
  • Occipital artery: runs in the occipital groove on the medial side of the mastoid process to reach the external occipital protuberance.

Introduction to the face (start of next topic)

  • The face has no deep fascia; its skin is connected to the underlying bones by loose connective tissue.
  • Facial muscles are embedded in the loose connective tissue (superficial fascia), and most insert into the skin.
  • All are supplied by the facial nerve.
  • They produce facial expressions (muscles of facial expression) and also control the facial orifices.

Orbicularis oculi (three parts: orbital, palpebral, lacrimal)

Orbital part: origin from the frontal process of the maxilla, with fibers forming loops around the orbital margin and returning to the origin; inserts into the skin of the eyelids above its origin; closes the eye tightly, as protection from intense light.

Key Points / Quick Review

Extent and layers

  • Eyebrows to superior nuchal lines; laterally to superior temporal line.
  • Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose areolar tissue, Pericranium.

Clinical points

  • Profuse bleeding: vessels adherent to fibrous septa cannot retract.
  • Loose areolar layer is dangerous: emissary veins lead to dural sinuses.
  • Hematoma spreads to upper eyelids (black eye).

Occipitofrontalis

  • Frontal bellies raise eyebrows; both bellies attach to the epicranial aponeurosis.
  • Occipital bellies arise from superior nuchal lines.

Nerves

  • Motor: temporal branch (front), posterior auricular (behind), both facial.
  • Front sensory: supratrochlear, supraorbital (V1), zygomatico-temporal (V2), auriculo-temporal (V3).
  • Behind: great auricular, lesser, greater and third occipital.

Arteries

  • Three in front: supratrochlear, supraorbital, superficial temporal.
  • Two behind: posterior auricular (gives stylomastoid), occipital.

Face (intro)

  • No deep fascia; muscles in superficial fascia, supplied by facial nerve.
  • Orbital part of orbicularis oculi closes the eye tightly.
